Good web design Pittsburgh PA customers respond to starts with a map, not a color palette. Pittsburgh is a city where people say they live in Bloomfield or Brookline before they say Pittsburgh, where a short trip can cross a river and go through a tunnel, and where "do you come out this far?" is a real question. A site that answers it in plain words, naming the neighborhoods you serve and the side of the river you work from, gives a customer a reason to call instead of scrolling on.

Dominion Web Design Pro writes every page by hand. Maurice Johnson builds the site, you see a free demo before you pay anything, and the price is printed: $497, $997 or $1,997, one time.

Ninety neighborhoods, each with a name people search

The City of Pittsburgh officially recognizes 90 neighborhoods, inside a city of about 307,600 people in the Census Bureau's estimate for July 2025. The system goes back to 1969, when the city created a Neighborhood Planning Division under Mayor Pete Flaherty. Some of the 90 are halves or thirds of a place locals treat as one: Squirrel Hill is split into North and South, and Lawrenceville into Upper, Central and Lower.

That matters for a small business because customers search the way they talk. Someone in Greenfield wants an HVAC tech who works Greenfield. Someone on the North Side may never drive to the South Hills for a haircut. A site that says only "serving Pittsburgh" leaves both of them guessing whether you are close enough to bother calling.

Rivers, hills and tunnels change what "nearby" means

The Heinz History Center calls Pittsburgh the City of Bridges and ties the nickname to three major rivers and a landscape full of hills and ravines. A 2006 study counted 446 bridges inside city limits, a figure people still argue about. Tunnels do the rest. PennDOT runs the Fort Pitt, Squirrel Hill, Liberty and Stowe tunnels, and WESA reported in 2017 that more than 229,000 people drove through them each day. The Fort Pitt and Squirrel Hill tunnels pinch the Parkway traffic at rush hour, and the Liberty Tunnels connect the South Hills to the city.

For a service business, that turns "within 15 miles" into a meaningless promise. Fifteen miles one way can be an easy drive; the other way can be two bridges and a backed-up tunnel. Here is how we would translate that onto a page.

What the customer wondersWhat the page should say
Will they come to my side of the river?The neighborhoods and boroughs you serve, named one by one, grouped by area.
How long until someone shows up?A realistic window for each area, written by you, not a radius in miles.
Do they charge more to cross town?Any trip charge or minimum, stated up front.
Where do I park if I come to them?Street, lot or garage, and the nearest bus line, in a sentence.

Web design Pittsburgh PA business streets ask for

Many of the city's neighborhoods have a main street with its own following. A site for a business on one of them should name the street early and plainly, because that is what regulars and visitors type.

  • Strip District and Lower LawrencevilleThe old warehouse and shipping ground along the Allegheny riverfront, now nicknamed Robotics Row for the robotics firms that moved into former factories there.
  • Butler Street, LawrencevilleWhere most of the neighborhood's shops, boutiques, galleries and restaurants sit.
  • Liberty Avenue, BloomfieldThe main strip of the neighborhood often called Pittsburgh's Little Italy, with Italian bakeries and restaurants mixed in among newer bars.
  • East Carson Street, South SideThe South Side's long main street and one of the city's busiest strips for restaurants, bars and nightlife.
  • Forbes and Murray Avenues, Squirrel HillThe two corridors where the neighborhood shops and eats.

Outside the city line the same rule holds. A customer in Mt. Lebanon or Cranberry searches for their own town, not for Pittsburgh, so a business that wants work there needs a page that says so and explains how it gets there.

Eds, meds and robots set the customer base

Pittsburgh's biggest employers are hospitals and universities. The Pittsburgh Business Times, as reported by WPXI, ranks UPMC as the region's largest employer and the largest nongovernmental employer in the state, with the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon also high on the list. Carnegie Mellon's National Robotics Engineering Center has been in Lawrenceville since 1996, and the robotics companies along the riverfront grew up partly around it.

Two kinds of small business feel this most. The first sells to the institutions and the tech firms: cleaning crews, caterers, electricians, sign shops, couriers. Their buyers check a site for a clear list of services, the areas covered and a way to request a quote, so that is what the site should lead with. The second sells to the people who work there, often on hospital shifts that run nights and weekends. For them, hours written as text, a tap-to-call number and a form that works at 2 a.m. count for more than anything decorative.

A Pittsburgh web designer, a developer or a company?

Searches for a Pittsburgh web designer, Pittsburgh web developers, website development in Pittsburgh and a Pittsburgh web design company often come from the same owner on the same afternoon. The useful question is narrower: do you need pages that win calls, or software that runs part of your business? For pages, one designer who writes and builds is usually enough. For software, hire developers with engineers on staff.

Dominion is the first kind. Maurice handles the writing, the build, the titles and descriptions, the sitemap and, on Pro and Agency, schema markup and Google Business Profile setup. There is no account manager in between, and no sales call to sit through first.

One owner, walked through

Picture a two-person house cleaning business based in Brookline. Most of its jobs are in the South Hills; it rarely takes work north of the rivers because the drive eats the day. Here is how we would set up its site, as an example rather than a client story.

  1. Say where you startThe home page names Brookline and the South Hills in the first lines, so the first question is answered at a glance.
  2. Draw the line honestlyThe service area page lists the neighborhoods and boroughs the business covers and says plainly which parts of town it does not.
  3. Give the busiest places their own pagesOn Pro, a few of the ten city pages go to the places where most bookings come from, each written about that place.
  4. Make booking easy on a phoneA short form asks for the address, the size of the home and the preferred day, and emails each request to the owner.

How local search reads a city of neighborhoods

Google says local results depend mainly on relevance, distance and prominence. In Pittsburgh, distance is especially blunt: a searcher in Shadyside sees businesses near Shadyside first. Prominence builds over time through reviews and mentions. Relevance is the part your site controls, and it improves when your pages and your Google Business Profile say clearly what you do and in which neighborhoods. Nobody can promise you a ranking, and we will not. We can make it obvious which part of Pittsburgh you serve.

Pittsburgh help worth calling first

  • Duquesne University SBDC. No-cost, confidential consulting and workshops for people starting or running a business in southwestern Pennsylvania, with outreach offices in Beaver, Butler and Lawrence counties.
  • University of Pittsburgh SBDC. Part of Pitt's Institute for Entrepreneurial Excellence, offering no-cost, confidential consulting to small businesses in Allegheny, Beaver, Greene, Indiana and Washington counties.
  • Urban Redevelopment Authority of Pittsburgh. With its partner Invest PGH, the URA offers low-interest loans of $5,000 to $500,000 to small and midsize businesses in the city, at fixed rates below market with terms of 5 to 20 years.
  • Greater Pittsburgh Chamber of Commerce. An affiliate of the Allegheny Conference on Community Development that advocates for business and works with more than two dozen local chambers across the 10-county region.

You are in good company. The SBA Office of Advocacy's 2024 profile counted 1.1 million small businesses in Pennsylvania, 99.6% of all businesses in the state, employing 45.4% of its workers.

Common questions

How much does web design cost in Pittsburgh, PA?

It ranges widely. Some designers quote a few hundred dollars for a template, others quote thousands for a custom project, and many will not give a figure until after a meeting. Our prices are printed: Starter is $497 for five hand-written pages, Pro is $997 for ten pages plus ten city or neighborhood pages, and Agency is $1,997 for research-led pages across your whole service area. Each is a one-time price. Hosting, maintenance and updates are $49 a month, or included while you keep an AI agent. The AI chat widget (Pro) or phone agent (Agency) is $297 a month after its free trial, and you can skip it.

What are normal web design rates for a small business?

Designers charge in three common ways: by the hour, by the project, or by the month on a subscription where you may never own the site. Hourly and monthly pricing make the final bill hard to predict. A flat project price is easier to plan around, as long as you know what is in it. Ours is flat and written down, and you own the finished site outright. Before you sign with anyone, ask who owns the domain and what happens if you stop paying.

Is there a Pittsburgh web design company that will meet me in person?

Yes, the city has local firms that do face-to-face meetings, and if that matters to you, hire one of them. We are not one. Dominion Web Design Pro is Maurice Johnson in East Texas, working by phone, email and shared links. What you get instead is the person who writes your pages answering your questions, and a free demo of your own site before you spend anything.

Do Pittsburgh web developers and web designers do the same job?

They overlap, but not entirely. A web designer plans and builds the pages your customers read. A developer writes software: logins, databases, custom ordering systems, tools tied to your inventory. Most neighborhood businesses need design with a solid build underneath, which is what we do. If you need custom software or an online store with a big catalog, that is a developer's project, and we will tell you before you buy.

Can my site have pages for neighborhoods on both sides of the river?

Yes, as long as you really work there. Pro includes ten city or neighborhood pages, each researched and written for that place, so a contractor could have one for Lawrenceville, one for the South Side and one for Mt. Lebanon. Agency begins with keyword research across your whole area to decide which places earn a page. We do not sell page counts: one honest page per place you serve beats a long list of names.

See your website before you pay for it

Give us your business name and what you do, and a demo site gets built for you to look at on your own phone. If you like it, pick a package. If you do not, you have spent nothing but the minute it took to look.
